prompt.context: Our client is a telecommunications infrastructure manufacturer and they have hired us to help determine if they have any excess manufacturing capacity. If there is any excess capacity, our client would like Booz Allen Hamilton to suggest a course of action to ensure they are profitable and efficient. The client currently has plants in both Minnesota and Mexico, close to the Texas border. The plants manufacture similar products and the facilities are about the same size. The company expanded capacity by replicating their first plant (using it as a template for others).
prompt.question: Does the client have excess manufacturing capacity, and if so, what course of action should they take to ensure profitability and efficiency?

clarifying_info.q: What are the operating hours of each plant?
clarifying_info.a: Each plant operates an 8am to 5pm shift. They have considered shifting to multiple shifts and running a 22-hour workday.

clarifying_info.q: What is the current utilization rate of the plants?
clarifying_info.a: They are running at fairly close to 100% utilization on the current single shift.

clarifying_info.q: What does overall demand look like in this industry?
clarifying_info.a: Demand is flat or declining. The US telecom market is relatively saturated with little new customer growth.

clarifying_info.q: What is the client's market share?
clarifying_info.a: The client has a relatively high market share of 80%.
Their direct clients are phone companies (telecom operators), since this is an infrastructure manufacturer.

clarifying_info.q: What are the switching costs in the industry?
clarifying_info.a: There are very high switching costs in the industry.

clarifying_info.q: Are there concerns about market share declining or new competitors entering?
clarifying_info.a: Our client recently acquired a competitor, so they are not anticipating big declines in market share. There are only a few competitors with little threat of new entrants due to flat or declining growth.

framework: Assess current capacity utilization: current shift hours, utilization rate per plant
Analyze demand outlook: industry growth trends, market saturation, client market share
Evaluate competitive landscape: number of players, switching costs, threat of new entrants, recent M&A
Determine if excess capacity exists based on demand vs. supply analysis
Identify options to address excess capacity: consolidation, shift expansion, contract manufacturing
Compare plant-level economics to determine which plants to retain (labor costs, distribution costs, quality)
Develop recommendation with risks and next steps

questions.prompt: Does the client have excess capacity? Walk through your reasoning.
questions.guidance: Strong answer identifies that (1) plants run only one 8-5 shift at ~100% utilization on that shift, so there is latent capacity if shifts are added; (2) demand is flat or declining, meaning total market volume will not absorb more output; (3) 80% market share and high switching costs make large share gains unlikely; therefore the existing two-plant footprint is over-sized relative to future demand. Candidate should explicitly state: yes, excess capacity exists because demand is shrinking while the plant network can be consolidated and run on extended shifts.

questions.prompt: How would you determine which plants to close?
questions.guidance: Candidate should propose comparing total cost per unit across plants. Key cost drivers to examine: (1) labor costs — most significant driver per interviewer; (2) distribution/logistics costs from each location (Mexico near Texas border vs. Minnesota proximity to US markets); (3) product quality consistency; (4) plant reconfiguration potential. Given that quality is consistent across plants and reconfiguration is not being considered, the decision hinges on labor and distribution costs.

questions.prompt: What is your recommendation on which plants to keep or close?
questions.guidance: Recommend closing the Minnesota plants and increasing utilization of Mexico plants by adding shifts (up to a 22-hour workday). Rationale: labor costs are the primary cost driver, and Mexican labor costs are lower. Consolidating into Mexico and running multi-shift operations can maintain output at lower cost.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the major risks and concerns of recommending the client close its Minnesota plants?

categories.name: Reputational / PR
ideas: Negative PR from closing US plants
Political backlash or government scrutiny over job losses
Employee morale impact at remaining facilities

categories.name: Operational / Scalability
ideas: Can Mexican plants quickly scale up capacity with additional shifts?
Risk of production bottlenecks during transition period
Single-location concentration risk if a disruption hits Mexico

categories.name: Quality
ideas: Quality consistency may be harder to maintain at higher utilization
Training and managing a larger workforce at one site

categories.name: Supply Chain / Distribution
ideas: Longer or more complex distribution routes to some US customers from Mexico
Currency and geopolitical risk of sole reliance on Mexico

recommendation: Close the Minnesota plants to eliminate excess fixed cost
Consolidate all manufacturing in Mexico and add shifts (move toward a 22-hour operating day) to maintain required output at lower labor cost
risks: Negative PR and political optics from shutting US plants
Scalability risk: Mexican plants may not be able to ramp quickly
Quality degradation risk at higher utilization and larger workforce
Single-region concentration risk — any disruption in Mexico halts all production
next_steps: Conduct detailed cost-per-unit analysis for each plant (labor, distribution, overhead)
Model transition timeline and capacity ramp plan for Mexico plants
Develop a workforce transition plan and communication strategy for Minnesota closures
Assess logistics and distribution network impact of single-country manufacturing
